overview.body:
**Candra** ​(*chandra*) — ‌The Glittering ‌Moon · ​Glittering, shining ​— the ​moon ​personified as ​a god ‌— belongs ​to the ​Sanskrit tradition, ‌where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Moon, Night, ​Soma". The ​name means ​"Glittering, ​shining — ​the moon ‌personified as ​a god; ‌also a ​name ‌of Soma ​in his ‌lunar aspect."[^1].

​**Candra** is ‌the moon ​personified: ​the glittering ‌lord whose ‌waxing and ‌waning marks ​the calendar, ​whose crescent ‌crowns ​Śiva’s hair, ​and whose ‌dynasty — ​the Candravamśa ​— produced, ‌by ​epic genealogy, ‌the Pāṇḍavas ​and Krishna ​himself. In ​the Veda ​he ‌is Soma’s ‌celestial body; ​in later ‌mythology he ​is the ​beautiful, cursed, ‌forever-waning ‌god.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ​**Candra** and ‌serves its ​temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/chandra/). The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *chandra* ​survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**चन्द्र**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Glittering, ‌shining — ​the ​moon personified ‌as ​a ‌god; also ​a ‌name of ​Soma ​in ​his lunar ​aspect."[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*chandra* ‌survives only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ​is ‌a ‌technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ​spelling. ‌The ​Unicode restoration ​**Candra** ‌recovers the ​full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ​the address ​bar. ‌The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— a ​description ​computed ‌from the ‌displayed ‌form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**c** ​→ **C** ​— ‌Same
- ​**h** → ​**—** ​— Not ‌written
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ​— ‌Same
- **n** ​→ ‌**n** ​— Same
- ‌**d** ​→ **d** ‌— ‌Same
- ​**r** → ​**r** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ˈtʃʌndrə/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Candra).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**C-** ​— ‌In IAST, ​c ‌is ​the ​English “ch” ​— ​palatal, ​never ‌a k-sound.
- ​**-an-** ‌— ​Short ‌a as ​in ‌“cup”; ​the ‌syllable is ​light.
- ​**-dra** ‌— ‌The cluster ‌dr; ​the ​name ‌means “glittering, ​shining”. ​In ‌Vedic ​the moon ​is ‌more ​often ‌Soma.

For ​the ​modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation ‌is: ​“CHUN-druh”

‌Kindred and ​historical ​forms ‌of ‌the name:

- ‌**Vedic** ‌— ​Soma ‌— the ​moon ​as ​the ‌soma-plant’s celestial ​home
- ​**Greek** ​— ‌Men, the ​lunar ​god ​of ‌the Anatolian ​coast

‌The ​lunar ‌dynasty of ​the ‌epics ‌— ​the Candravamśa ​— ​traces ​every ‌lunar king ‌to ​him.

domains.body:
**Candra** ​is the ‌moon ‌personified: the ​glittering ​lord whose ​waxing ​and waning ​marks ‌the calendar, ​whose ​crescent crowns ‌Śiva’s ​hair, and ‌whose ​dynasty — ‌the ​Candravamśa — ​produced, ​by epic ​genealogy, ​the Pāṇḍavas ‌and ​Krishna himself. ‌In ​the Veda ‌he ​is Soma’s ‌celestial ​body; in ‌later ​mythology he ​is ‌the beautiful, ‌cursed, ‌forever-waning god.[^1]

### ​The ​Waxing Fortnight

‌The ​bright half ​of ‌the month, ​śuklapakṣa, ​is his ‌growth ​— the ‌calendar’s ​first engine.

### ​Śiva’s ​Diadem

The ​crescent ‌moon in ‌Śiva’s ​hair is ‌Candra’s ​seat — ​cooled ‌by the ‌Ganges, ‌crowned by ‌it.

### ​Father of ‌Budha

​By Tārā, ​wife ​of Bṛhaspati, ‌he ​fathered Budha ​— ​Mercury and ‌ancestor ​of the ​lunar ​line.

### The ‌Waning ​Curse

Cursed ‌by ​Dakṣa to ‌waste ​away for ‌loving ‌Tārā, he ​is ​saved by ​Śiva’s ​partial mercy ‌— ‌hence the ​phases.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Candra ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Waxing ​Fortnight** ​— ​The ‌bright half ​of ‌the ​month, ‌śuklapakṣa, ​is ‌his growth ​— ‌the ​calendar’s ​first ‌engine.
- ‌**Śiva’s ‌Diadem** — ​The ​crescent ‌moon ​in ​Śiva’s ‌hair is ​Candra’s ​seat ‌— ​cooled ‌by ​the Ganges, ​crowned ​by ​it.
- ‌**Father ‌of ​Budha** — ‌By ​Tārā, ​wife ‌of ‌Bṛhaspati, ‌he ‌fathered Budha ​— ‌Mercury ​and ​ancestor ​of ‌the lunar ​line.
- ​**The ​Waning ‌Curse** ​— ​Cursed by ​Dakṣa ‌to ​waste ‌away ​for ‌loving ​Tārā, he ‌is ‌saved ​by ​Śiva’s ​partial ​mercy — ‌hence ‌the ​phases.

mythology.body:
Candra’s mythology ​clusters around two ‌stories: the theft ‌of Tārā and ​its curse, and ​the moon-churning of ​the ocean of ​milk. He is ​the most beautiful ‌of the gods ​and the most ​diminished — the ‌waxing and waning ​written into his ‌body as punishment ​and mercy at once.[^1]

### ‌The Abduction of ​Tārā (Purāṇic Cycle)

​Candra loved Tārā, ​wife of the ​guru Bṛhaspati, and ​carried her off; ‌the gods’ war ​over her ended ‌with her return ​— and her ‌pregnancy, which she ​refused to explain ‌until the child’s ​radiance declared the ‌moon his father. ​Budha, the child, ​founded the lunar ‌dynasty through which ‌the epic’s heroes ‌descend.[^2]

### The Curse ​and the Mercy ​(Śiva Cycle)

Dakṣa, ‌Bṛhaspati’s champion, cursed ​the moon to ​waste to nothing; ‌the pleading gods ​won a partial ​reprieve — the ‌curse would lift for ​half each month. ‌The phases of ​the moon are ​the scar of ​the love-affair, and ​Śiva’s wearing of ‌the crescent is ‌the war-god’s mercy ​made ornament.

### The ‌Moon from the ​Churning (Samudra Manthana)

​When the gods ‌and demons churned ‌the ocean of ‌milk for the ‌nectar of immortality, ​the moon rose ‌among the treasures ​— Dhanvantari’s medicine-chest, ​the apsarases, and ​Candra, the glittering ‌disc. Śiva took ​him onto his ​brow; the poison ​of the churning, ‌Halāhala, he drank ​instead, turning his ​throat blue.

### The ​Celestial Plant (Vedic Soma)

‌In the Veda ​the moon is ‌Soma’s home: the ​pressed plant’s juice ‌ascends to become ​the lunar disc, ‌and the moon’s ‌quarters are the ​soma-cup’s refills. The ​identification of moon, ​plant, and god ​is the Veda’s ‌most compact theology ‌— three substances, ​one divinity.
